expectedText:
VOLUNTARY DECLARATION OF PARENTAGE
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

DECLARATION OF INTENT TO ESTABLISH PARENTAGE
Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee state that Riley Lee is their child, and that they intend by signing this document to voluntarily and jointly establish Morgan Casey Lee's legal parentage of Riley Lee, without a court proceeding, through the process described in this document.

LEGISLATIVE BASIS AND LEGAL EFFECT OF A VOLUNTARY DECLARATION
California's Legislature has found a compelling state interest in establishing parentage for all children, treating establishment of parentage as "the first step toward a child support award" and the gateway to benefits including social security, health insurance, survivors' benefits, military benefits, and inheritance rights. California law further provides that a completed voluntary declaration of parentage that complies with statutory requirements and is filed with the state child support agency "is equivalent to a judgment of parentage of the child and confers on the declarant all rights and duties of a parent," subject to the statute's own listed exceptions (void declarations, rescission, later challenge, and minor-signer rules).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "There is a compelling state interest in establishing parentage for all children. Establishing parentage is the first step toward a child support award, which, in turn, provides children with equal rights and access to benefits, including, but not limited to, social security, health insurance, survivors' benefits, military benefits, and inheritance rights."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7570(a) (California Legislative Information text), the legislative findings (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7570.)
  "Except as provided in Sections 7573.5, 7575, 7576, 7577, and 7580, a completed voluntary declaration of parentage that complies with this chapter and that has been filed with the Department of Child Support Services is equivalent to a judgment of parentage of the child and confers on the declarant all rights and duties of a parent."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7573(d) (California Legislative Information text), a completed declaration's judgment-equivalent effect (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7573.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a voluntary-parentage-declaration system is structured and what legal weight such a declaration can carry — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parentage declaration, nor a claim that every jurisdiction uses this same mechanism, timeline, or effect. Whether a voluntary declaration is available at all, what form it must take, and what legal effect it carries varies by state.

WHO SIGNS, AND THE WITNESSING REQUIREMENT
Under California's model, a voluntary declaration must be signed by both the woman who gave birth to the child and the other person seeking to establish parentage, and the signatures must be attested by a notary or witnessed. At a hospital birth, hospital staff are the typical witness, and are required to forward the signed declaration to the Department of Child Support Services within 20 days of the date the declaration was signed. Signing is not limited to the hospital — if it is not completed there, it may be completed by the attesting parents, notarized, and mailed to the Department of Child Support Services at any time after the child's birth.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Staff in the hospital shall witness the signatures of parents signing a voluntary declaration of parentage and shall forward the signed declaration to the Department of Child Support Services within 20 days of the date the declaration was signed."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7571(a) (California Legislative Information text), hospital-staff witnessing and the 20-day forwarding requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7571.)
  "A voluntary declaration of parentage shall be in a record signed by the woman who gave birth to the child and by either the only possible genetic parent other than the woman who gave birth or the intended parent of a child conceived through assisted reproduction, and the signatures shall be attested by a notary or witnessed."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7573(b) (California Legislative Information text), who must sign and the attestation requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7573.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a voluntary-declaration signing and witnessing process can be structured — not a claim about which state's law governs the signing of any specific declaration. Who must sign, who may serve as a witness, and whether notarization is an alternative to witnessing all vary by state.

WHEN A COMPETING PRESUMED PARENT ALREADY EXISTS
California's voluntary-declaration statute does not operate independently of the state's marital and other parentage presumptions — it builds in a specific disqualifying condition. A declaration is void from the outset if, at the time of signing, a person other than the woman who gave birth to the child or the person seeking to establish parentage through the declaration is already a presumed parent under the marital presumption or one of the statute's other presumed-parent categories.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A voluntary declaration of parentage is void if, at the time of signing, any of the following are true: (1) A person other than the woman who gave birth to the child or a person seeking to establish parentage through a voluntary declaration of parentage is a presumed parent under Section 7540 or subdivision (a), (b), or (c) of Section 7611."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7573.5(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), voidness when a competing presumed parent already exists (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7573.5.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory subsection (§ 7573.5(a)(1)); no additional independent source was found for this. It is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a voluntary-declaration mechanism can be built to yield to an existing marital or other statutory presumption of parentage for a different person rather than override it — not a claim about whether any such competing presumption exists, or how it would be resolved, in any specific case or jurisdiction. Whether a marital or other presumption blocks use of a voluntary declaration, and how that conflict is resolved, varies by state.

STATEMENT REGARDING OTHER POSSIBLE PARENTS
Jordan Alex Lee states that, to Jordan Alex Lee's knowledge, no other person is married to Jordan Alex Lee or otherwise legally presumed to be a parent of Riley Lee, and that Morgan Casey Lee is the only other person being asked to sign this document as Riley Lee's parent.

WHAT THE DECLARATION ESTABLISHES — AND WHAT IT DOES NOT
A completed, filed declaration is equivalent to a judgment of parentage and confers on the declarant all rights and duties of a parent. Separately, California's statute repeatedly treats custody, visitation, and support as governed by their own court orders rather than by the declaration itself — for example, an order for custody, visitation, or child support remains in effect until a court determines the declaration should be set aside, subject to the court's power to modify the order as otherwise provided by law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Except as provided in Sections 7573.5, 7575, 7576, 7577, and 7580, a completed voluntary declaration of parentage that complies with this chapter and that has been filed with the Department of Child Support Services is equivalent to a judgment of parentage of the child and confers on the declarant all rights and duties of a parent."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7573(d) (California Legislative Information text), the declaration's judgment-equivalent effect on parentage itself (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7573.)
  "An order for custody, visitation, or child support shall remain in effect until the court determines that the voluntary declaration of parentage should be set aside, subject to the court's power to modify the orders as otherwise provided by law."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7577(j)(2) (California Legislative Information text), custody/visitation/support orders remain separately governed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7577.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a jurisdiction can structure its voluntary-declaration system so that establishing parentage and setting custody, visitation, or support terms are treated as distinct steps — not a claim about how custody, visitation, or support would be established for any specific child, and not a claim that a signed declaration does or does not itself create enforceable custody or support terms. Whether — and how — a parentage declaration interacts with custody, visitation, and support determinations varies by state.

THE RESCISSION PERIOD AFTER SIGNING
California law gives either signer a defined window to undo an already-signed declaration by filing a rescission form, rather than by going to court: either parent may rescind the voluntary declaration of parentage by filing a rescission form with the Department of Child Support Services within 60 days of the date of execution of the declaration by the attesting parents, whichever signature is later, unless a court order for custody, visitation, or child support has already been entered in an action in which the signatory seeking to rescind was a party.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Either parent may rescind the voluntary declaration of parentage by filing a rescission form with the Department of Child Support Services within 60 days of the date of execution of the declaration by the attesting parents, whichever signature is later, unless a court order for custody, visitation, or child support has been entered in an action in which the signatory seeking to rescind was a party."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7575(a) (California Legislative Information text), the 60-day rescission window and its cutoff condition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7575.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory section (§ 7575); no additional independent source was found for this. It is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a voluntary-declaration system can include a short, self-service rescission window with a specific triggering condition (a later court order in a case the rescinding signer was a party to) — not a claim about which state's law governs the rescission of any specific declaration. Whether a rescission period exists at all, how long it runs, how it is counted (from signing versus from filing), and what cuts it off differ significantly by state; this is exactly the kind of date-sensitive fact that does not transfer across jurisdictions.

LATER CHALLENGE BY A SIGNER AFTER RESCISSION CLOSES
After the rescission window closes, California law still allows a signer of the declaration to bring a court challenge, but only on narrow grounds and only within a further fixed outer deadline: not later than two years after the declaration's effective date, a signatory may commence a proceeding to challenge it on the basis of fraud, duress, or material mistake of fact. That two-year outer limit does not apply if the declaration was void from the start.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "After the period for rescission provided in Section 7575 expires, but not later than two years after the effective date provided in subdivision (c) of Section 7573 of a voluntary declaration of parentage, a signatory of the voluntary declaration of parentage may commence a proceeding to challenge the declaration on the basis of fraud, duress, or material mistake of fact."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7576(a) (California Legislative Information text), the two-year outer deadline and the fraud/duress/mistake grounds (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7576.)
  "The limitations period provided in subdivision (a) shall not apply if the voluntary declaration of parentage is void under Section 7573.5."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7576(b) (California Legislative Information text), the exception for a declaration that was void from the start (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7576.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory section (§ 7576); no additional independent source was found for this. It is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a voluntary-declaration system can pair a short rescission window with a longer, narrower, outer challenge deadline for the people who signed — not a claim about which state's law, grounds, or deadline governs any specific challenge. The statutory text of this section names fraud, duress, and material mistake of fact as the grounds for a signer's post-rescission challenge; it does not itself state that genetic testing must accompany that challenge or that a "best interest of the child" standard applies to it — that best-interest standard is expressly written into a different section governing challenges brought by non-signatories, and this clause does not extend that standard to signer challenges without a textual basis for doing so. Grounds, deadlines, and any best-interest overlay for challenging a signed declaration vary by state.

GENETIC TESTING IN A NON-SIGNER'S CHALLENGE
California's statute ties a right to expedited genetic testing to one specific kind of challenge — one brought by someone who did not sign the declaration and who claims standing as an alleged genetic parent. If the court holds a hearing to determine that person's standing, the hearing must be held on an expedited basis, and if the person challenging the declaration is an alleged genetic parent, genetic testing must be ordered on an expedited basis.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "If the court holds a hearing to determine standing, the hearing shall be held on an expedited basis. If the person challenging the voluntary declaration of parentage is an alleged genetic parent, genetic testing shall be ordered on an expedited basis."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7577(c) (California Legislative Information text), expedited genetic testing for a non-signatory's standing challenge (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7577.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory subsection (§ 7577(c)); no additional independent source was found for this. It is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a voluntary-declaration system can attach an expedited genetic-testing right to a non-signer's standing challenge — not a claim about whether genetic testing is available, required, or excluded in any specific challenge or jurisdiction. This statute's own text does not extend this genetic-testing provision to the separate signer's-challenge mechanism described elsewhere in this document; whether, and on what terms, genetic testing is available in a signer's own post-rescission challenge varies by state and was not confirmed by this research.

TIMING RULES WHEN A SIGNER IS A MINOR
California's statute delays both the effective date and the rescission clock when a signer is a minor. A voluntary declaration signed by a minor parent does not establish parentage until 60 days after both signatories have reached 18 years of age or are emancipated, whichever first occurs. The rescission right tracks that same delay: a person who signs as a minor may rescind at any time up to 60 days after that signatory reaches 18 or becomes emancipated, whichever first occurs.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Notwithstanding subdivision (c) of Section 7573, a voluntary declaration of parentage that is signed by a minor parent does not establish parentage until 60 days after both signatories have reached 18 years of age or are emancipated, whichever first occurs."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7580(a) (California Legislative Information text), delayed effective date for a minor signer (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7580.)
  "A person who signs a voluntary declaration of parentage as a minor may rescind the voluntary declaration of parentage at any time up to 60 days after the signatory reaches 18 years of age or becomes emancipated, whichever first occurs."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7580(b) (California Legislative Information text), the extended rescission right for a minor signer (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7580.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory subsection (§ 7580); no additional independent source was found for this. It is used as real evidence that a voluntary-declaration system can adjust both the effective date and the rescission timeline when a signer is a minor — not a claim about which state's law governs a declaration signed by a minor, or about the age, emancipation status, or timeline applicable in any specific case. Whether minor-signer rules exist at all, and how they alter timing, varies by state.

SIGNATURE BLOCK
Signed by Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________

Signed by Morgan Casey Lee: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________

This document is signed in the presence of a witness or notary, consistent with the witnessing or notarization requirement described elsewhere in this document; the identity and role of the witness or notary are recorded separately.
